# G4 gate (b) — hand-verified `.eml` fixture corpus

Wave brief `brief-y4-mail.md`, spike gate 2 (J2, ruling 6; sprint plan's G4).
Sibling record: `SPIKE-G4.md` (gate a's deny-gate history and gate c's
footprint delta). The Y2 corpus (`tests/fixtures/anydoc_corpus/MANIFEST.md`)
is the named pattern; this file follows its shape.

## Why this file exists, and in what order it was produced

The wave brief requires the fixture corpus and its expected counts to be
fixed **before the candidate parser runs even once** against them. No mail
adapter exists in this repo as of this commit, so the counts in
`manifest.json` cannot have been produced by running `mail-parser` and
copying its answer. They were produced the only way that satisfies the gate
honestly, in this order:

1. Every `.eml` fixture was **hand-authored as raw RFC 5322/MIME text**, not
   exported from a mail client and not generated by any mail library —
   `build_mail_fixtures.py` (beside this file) shows exactly what bytes went
   into each fixture. Where a fixture needed an *encoded* form (RFC 2047
   header words, quoted-printable, base64), the script started from a chosen
   plaintext, mechanically encoded it, and printed the plaintext it used —
   so the "expected" answer was fixed at authoring time, before any decoder
   touched the bytes.
2. `manifest.json` records that hand-known answer, per fixture, per field,
   with each field's meaning defined once in `manifest.json`'s
   `counting_rules`, worded so a reader can open a fixture in a text editor
   and reach the same number without knowing anything about `mail-parser`'s
   own internal vocabulary.
3. The hand-typed answer was then **independently cross-checked** — not
   just re-read — using Python's standard-library `email` package
   (`verify_with_stdlib_email.py`, transcript `stdlib-email-crosscheck.txt`),
   a wholly different implementation from both the authoring script and from
   `mail-parser`. Every header count, address count, decoded Subject/From,
   decoded body text (including the windows-1252→Unicode round-trip), and
   attachment length that `manifest.json` claims matches this second,
   independent tool's output exactly.
4. **Only after both (1) and (3) agreed** was `mail-parser` run once,
   diagnostically, against the whole corpus, from a throwaway scratch crate
   outside this repository (`mail-parser-diagnostic-probe.rs`,
   `mail-parser-diagnostic-run.txt`) — never as committed extraction code,
   and never as the source of any number in `manifest.json`. This is
   evidence for the adopt/escalate call, not part of the hand-verification
   itself.

## Pass criterion

**Exact match, per fixture, per field in `manifest.json`.** A future
extractor's test suite loads `manifest.json` and asserts every count
verbatim. For `06-malformed-no-headers.eml` (`"valid": false`): refusal to
produce a message at all is the only passing outcome — any body/attachment
output, partial or otherwise, is a failure of that fixture, not a skip and
not partial credit.

## One field corrected in Y4 (the adoption wave, not this spike)

`04-nested-rfc822.eml`'s `nested_message.body_text_decoded` originally read
with no trailing `\r\n`. Building `src/runtime/atlas/mail.rs`'s own test
suite against this fixture found the fixture's own bytes carry two CRLFs
before `--NEST-BOUNDARY-04--` (one blank line); RFC 2046 §5.1.1 consumes only
the LAST CRLF as the boundary delimiter, so the other is the nested body's
own final line terminator — real content, not a parser artifact. Verified
two ways, independent of `mail-parser`: a direct read of the fixture's raw
bytes, and Python's stdlib `email` package (the same independent tool
`verify_with_stdlib_email.py` already uses) decoding this exact nested
payload — both agree the trailing `\r\n` belongs. Corrected in place, with
the full reasoning recorded beside the field itself
(`manifest.json`'s own `body_text_decoded_correction_note`), per this
codebase's own precedent for a correction found while building real code
against a fixture (`archive.rs`'s own module doc carries the same shape of
correction against its research note). No other field, on this fixture or
any other, is affected.

## What each fixture covers

| Fixture | Covers |
|---|---|
| `01-plain-text.eml` | Plain text message, no MIME multipart structure |
| `02-multipart-alternative.eml` | `multipart/alternative` with both a text/plain and a text/html body |
| `03-with-attachment.eml` | A message with one base64-encoded attachment (`report.txt`) alongside a text body |
| `04-nested-rfc822.eml` | A `message/rfc822` part nested one level inside an outer message (a mail inside a mail), itself carrying its own full header set and body |
| `05-encoding-zoo.eml` | Quoted-printable body text in a non-UTF-8 charset (windows-1252, including a byte — `€` at `0x80` — that is not Latin-1-compatible), a base64 binary attachment, an RFC 2047 UTF-8 B-encoded Subject, and an RFC 2047 ISO-8859-1 Q-encoded From display-name |
| `06-malformed-no-headers.eml` | Deliberately malformed: no RFC 5322 header field line anywhere in the file, so the only honest outcome is a hard parse failure |

Every exact count is in `manifest.json`, not restated here, so there is
exactly one place that can drift.

## `diagnostic-not-manifest-broken-mime.eml` — not part of the exact-match corpus

Not one of the six required fixtures, and `manifest.json` makes no claim
about it (same status as Y2's fixture 06, "hostile entry expansion"). A
**well-formed RFC 5322 envelope** (valid From/To/Subject/Date/Message-ID/
MIME-Version/Content-Type — 7 headers, same shape as the valid fixtures
above) whose declared `multipart/mixed` boundary is opened
(`--BROKEN`) but never closed (no matching `--BROKEN--` and no second
`--BROKEN`) — a different failure shape from `06`'s "no headers at all".

It exists because gate (b)'s diagnostic `mail-parser` run produced a
materially different outcome on this input than on `06`, and that
difference is the single most important finding of this gate for the
adopt/escalate call — see `SPIKE-G4.md`, gate (b), "A caveat found
empirically." Recorded here as a byte-exact fixture rather than only
described in prose, so the claim is checkable.

## `07-genuine-html-only.eml` — not part of the exact-match corpus

Not one of the six required fixtures, and `manifest.json` makes no claim
about it (same status as `diagnostic-not-manifest-broken-mime.eml`,
above). Added downstream of the spike, in the adoption wave, as a
regression pin for a review finding: a single part, physically
`text/html`, with no `multipart/alternative` wrapper and no `text/plain`
part anywhere in the wire bytes — the mirror image of `01-plain-text.eml`.
`mail-parser` aliases this single part into both `text_body` and
`html_body` exactly as it does for `01`'s plain-text part (module doc on
`mail.rs`, caveat 2, case (a)), so `mail.rs`'s own genuineness check must
tell the two shapes apart by the aliased part's own physical type, not by
index equality alone — an earlier version of that check always trusted
the text side on a collision, which is right for `01` and backwards for
this fixture. See `src/runtime/atlas/mail.rs`'s own
`fixture_07_html_only_message_keeps_genuine_html_and_never_gains_fake_text`
test.

## Reproducing this corpus

```sh
python3 tests/fixtures/mail_corpus/build_mail_fixtures.py   # writes the 6 fixtures + prints the plaintext each encoding started from
python3 tests/fixtures/mail_corpus/verify_with_stdlib_email.py  # independent cross-check, stdlib email package
```

Both scripts are deterministic and touch nothing outside
`tests/fixtures/mail_corpus/`; neither depends on Cargo, `mail-parser`, or
any Rust toolchain.
